about.title: Fremont Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Fremont's workforce is spread across manufacturing floors, warehouse docks, construction sites and delivery routes, and a job injury in any of those settings raises the same first question: who is actually responsible for making you whole? In California, your employer's workers' compensation coverage usually handles medical care and partial wage replacement no matter who was at fault. That system, though, is generally the only claim you can bring against the employer itself. A separate injury case becomes possible when someone outside your company contributed to the harm — a subcontractor sharing the site, the owner of a property you were servicing, the maker of a machine that failed, or another driver who hit you while you were on the clock. That last category matters here. Fremont recorded 799 injury collisions in 2025, with 1,069 people hurt, and I-880, I-680 and Fremont Boulevard are corridors Alameda County workers travel every shift. LawProactive is not a law firm. We simply connect you, at no cost, with an independent attorney who can sort out which claims fit your situation.

whyChoose.title: Why Fremont Workers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: We Look Beyond Workers' Comp
items.desc: Workers' compensation is usually your only remedy against your employer, but it does not cover everything. The attorneys we connect you with examine whether a subcontractor, property owner, equipment manufacturer or another driver bears separate responsibility.

items.title: Deadlines Are Handled Early
items.desc: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, and any third-party injury claim generally carries a two-year filing window. Getting connected quickly keeps both clocks from becoming a problem.

items.title: Retaliation Is Not Something You Accept
items.desc: Firing, demoting or punishing an employee for reporting an injury is illegal in California. If your Fremont employer has pushed back after you spoke up, that is worth raising with the attorney you are matched with.

items.question: I was hit on I-880 while driving for work in Fremont. Do I only get workers' comp?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Because you were working, workers' compensation should cover your medical treatment and part of your lost wages regardless of fault. If another driver caused the crash, California law also allows a separate injury claim against that driver, which can address losses workers' comp does not reach. An independent attorney can evaluate both paths at the same time.

items.question: Can I sue my employer directly for a workplace injury in California?
items.answer: In most situations, no. Workers' compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer, even when the employer was careless. The exceptions are narrow, so the more common route to a fuller recovery is a claim against a negligent third party such as a subcontractor, a property owner or an equipment maker.

items.question: What if I waited a few weeks to tell my Alameda County employer about the injury?
items.answer: California expects you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, so do it in writing as soon as you can if you have not already. A late report can complicate benefits, but it does not automatically end your options. Any third-party claim runs on its own two-year deadline, and an attorney can help you understand where you stand.
